items.q: In circulating blood, thyroid hormone levels show that T4 is present in maximum concentration, approximately ___ that of T3.
items.exp: Circulating T4 is present in maximum concentration, approximately 10 times that of T3 (10 x T3). (Book p902)

items.q: Match the thyroid hormone carrier proteins to their respective binding percentages — 1) Thyroid Binding Globulin (TBG) 2) Albumin 3) Transthyretin … A) 70% B) 20% C) 10%
items.exp: Thyroid hormone carrier proteins bind circulating hormone in the proportions: TBG 70%, Albumin 20%, and Transthyretin 10%. (Book p902)

items.q: In the opening classification of hyperthyroxinemia (elevated T3 and T4 levels), what biochemical finding defines thyrotoxicosis rather than euthyroid hyperthyroxinemia?
opts: Elevated free T3 and free T4 levels
Elevated total T3 and total T4 levels with normal free hormone
Isolated elevated thyroglobulin with normal TSH
items.exp: Hyperthyroxinemia branches into thyrotoxicosis (defined by elevated free T3/free T4) and euthyroid hyperthyroxinemia (elevated total T3/total T4). (Book p902)

items.q: Under thyrotoxicosis with elevated free hormone levels, match the gland status to its underlying mechanism — 1) Overworking gland 2) Normal gland … A) Hyperthyroidism B) Stored hormones released / Hormone supplement
items.exp: In thyrotoxicosis, an overworking gland corresponds to true hyperthyroidism, whereas a normal gland releases stored hormones (thyroiditis) or receives exogenous hormone supplementation. (Book p902)

items.q: Assess these causes of euthyroid hyperthyroxinemia (elevated total T3 and total T4): I TBG excess. II Drugs that inhibit deiodinase-2 (D1-2), Sick euthyroid syndrome, and RTH.
opts: Both I and II are true
I is true; II is false
I is false; II is true
Both I and II are false
items.exp: Causes of euthyroid hyperthyroxinemia listed on page 902 include: 1) TBG excess, 2) Drugs that inhibit deiodinase-2, 3) Sick euthyroid syndrome, and 4) RTH. (Book p902)

items.q: Which of the following is NOT listed on page 902 as a cause of TBG excess?
opts: Chronic active hepatitis and inherited TBG excess (rare)
items.exp: Causes of TBG excess on page 902 are OCPs, estrogen, pregnancy, steroids, chronic active hepatitis, and inherited TBG excess (rare). Nephrotic syndrome causes urinary protein loss and low TBG. (Book p902)

items.q: A 24-year-old woman taking oral contraceptive pills has high total T4 and total T3 on routine screening. Free T4, free T3, and TSH are normal. What is the diagnosis?
opts: Euthyroid hyperthyroxinemia due to TBG excess
Primary thyrotoxicosis from an overworking gland
items.exp: OCPs raise TBG levels, leading to elevated total T3/T4 with normal free hormone levels, classified as euthyroid hyperthyroxinemia. (Book p902)

items.q: What is the primary pathogenesis of Resistance to Thyroid Hormone (RTH)?
opts: Partial or complete resistance of T3/T4 receptors leading to uninhibited increase of TSH with high T3/T4 but no action
Activating mutation in the TSH receptor causing autonomous thyroid follicle hyperplasia
Deiodinase-2 deficiency in the liver preventing peripheral hormone degradation
Circulating autoantibodies that block thyroid binding globulin clearance
items.exp: In RTH, partial or completely resistant T3/T4 receptors cause uninhibited increase of TSH, producing high T3 and T4 that fail to exert downstream action. (Book p902)

items.q: Match the clinical presentation of Resistance to Thyroid Hormone (RTH) to its relative frequency — 1) Euthyroid state 2) Toxicosis … A) Most common (m/c) B) Rare (due to resistance to TR-β forms)
items.exp: Clinically in RTH, patients are most commonly euthyroid; toxicosis is rare and occurs due to resistance to beta forms (TR-β). (Book p902)

items.q: In Resistance to Thyroid Hormone (RTH), the rare occurrence of toxicosis is due to resistance specifically involving ___ forms of the receptor.
items.exp: Toxicosis in RTH is rare and develops due to selective resistance to beta forms (TR-β). (Book p902)

items.q: A male infant presents with severe cognitive impairment and hypotonia. Molecular genetic testing identifies a loss-of-function defect in the neuronal MCT8 transporter. What is the diagnosis?
items.exp: MCT8 defect causes impaired entry of T3 into neurons, producing Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome characterized by severe cognitive impairment. (Book p902)

items.q: In the CNS thyroid hormone transport pathway: I T4 crosses the blood-brain barrier via OATP1C1 and MCT8 into astrocytes, where D2 converts it to T3. II T3 enters neurons via MCT8 to activate T3-responsive genes.
opts: Both I and II are true
I is true; II is false
I is false; II is true
Both I and II are false
items.exp: T4 crosses the blood-brain barrier via OATP1C1/MCT8 into astrocytes where deiodinase-2 (D2) converts T4 to T3; T3 then enters neurons via MCT8 to regulate T3-responsive genes. (Book p902)

items.q: Which transporter protein is shown alongside MCT8 at the blood-brain barrier for thyroid hormone transport into astrocytes on page 902?
items.exp: The blood-brain barrier diagram depicts OATP1C1 and MCT8 facilitating thyroid hormone transport into astrocytes. (Book p902)
